'''Henry Stephen Rzepa''' (born 1950)<ref name=dob/> is a chemist and [[Emeritus]] [[Professor]] of [[Computational Chemistry]] at [[Imperial College London]].<ref name="interview">{{cite web|url=http://www.rsc.org/Publishing/ChemScience/Volume/2009/05/Henry_Rzepa_interview.asp |title=A Royal Society of Chemistry interview with Henry Rzepa |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121019053740/http://www.rsc.org/Publishing/ChemScience/Volume/2009/05/Henry_Rzepa_interview.asp |archive-date=2012-10-19 }}</ref>{{cn|date=September 2024}}

==Education==
Rzepa was born in 1950 and was educated at [[Wandsworth Comprehensive School]] in London. He then entered the chemistry department at [[Imperial College London]] where he graduated in 1971. He stayed to do a [[Ph.D.]] on the [[physical organic]] chemistry of [[indole]]s supervised by Brian Challis.<ref name=rzphd>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|publisher=[[University of London]]|title=Hydrogen transfer reactions of indoles|first= Henry Stephen|last=Rzepa|date=1974|url=http://ethos.bl.uk/OrderDetails.do?uin=uk.bl.ethos.471287|website=ethos.bl.uk|oclc=930651784|hdl=10044/1/20860|doi=10.5281/zenodo.18777}}</ref><ref name=ChallisRzepa1975>{{cite journal|last1=Challis|first1=Brian C.|last2=Rzepa|first2=Henry S.|title=Heteroaromatic hydrogen exchange reactions. Part VIII. The ionisation of 1,3-dimethylindolin-2-one|journal=Journal of the Chemical Society, Perkin Transactions 2|issue=15|year=1975|pages=1822|issn=0300-9580|doi=10.1039/p29750001822|url=http://spiral.imperial.ac.uk/bitstream/10044/1/21275/2/p29750001822.pdf|hdl=10044/1/21275}}</ref>

==Career and research==
After spending three years doing [[postdoctoral research]] at [[University of Texas at Austin]], Texas with [[Michael J. S. Dewar|Michael Dewar]]<ref name=dewar>{{cite journal|last1=Dewar|first1=M. J. S.|author-link1=Michael J. S. Dewar|last2=Mckee|first2=M. L.|last3=Rzepa|first3=H. S.|title=ChemInform Abstract: MNDO Parameters for third period elements|journal=Chemischer Informationsdienst|volume=9|issue=34|year=1978|issn=0009-2975|doi=10.1002/chin.197834001}}</ref> in the emerging field of [[computational chemistry]], he returned to Imperial College and was eventually appointed as [[Professor]] of the college in 2003. {{As of|2017}} he is Emeritus Professor of Computational Chemistry.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ukoln.ac.uk/web-focus/events/workshops/wiki-workshop-2006/people/|title= Information on conference speakers|website=ukoln.ac.uk}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://rzepa.net/cv_bio.html|title=Rzepa Biography|website=rzepa.net}}</ref>{{cn|date=September 2024}}

His research interests<ref name="googlescholar">{{Google scholar id}}</ref> directed towards combining different types of chemical information tools for solving structural, mechanistic and [[stereochemical]] problems in [[organic chemistry|organic]], [[bioorganic chemistry|bioorganic]], [[organometallic chemistry]] and [[catalysis]], using techniques such as [[Computational Chemistry#Semi-empirical methods|semiempirical]] [[molecular orbital]] methods (the [[MNDO]] family), [[Nuclear magnetic resonance|Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR)]] spectroscopy, [[X-ray crystallography]] and ''[[ab initio quantum chemistry methods|ab initio]]'' quantum theories. Aware of the complex semantic issues involved in converging different areas of chemistry to address modern multidisciplinary problems, he started investigating the use of the [[Internet]] as an information and integrating medium around 1987, focusing in 1994 on the [[World Wide Web]] as having the most potential.<ref name="Rzepa1994">{{cite journal|last1=Rzepa|first1=Henry S.|last2=Whitaker|first2=Benjamin J.|last3=Winter|first3=Mark J.|title=Chemical applications of the World-Wide-Web system|journal=Journal of the Chemical Society, Chemical Communications|issue=17|year=1994|pages=1907|issn=0022-4936|doi=10.1039/c39940001907|s2cid=95897719}}</ref> [[Peter Murray-Rust]] and he first introduced [[Chemical Markup Language|Chemical Markup Language (CML)]] in 1995 as a rich carrier of semantic chemical information and data; and they coined the term ''Datument'' as a [[portmanteau]] word to better express the evolution from the [[document]]s produced by traditional [[academic publishing]] methods to the [[Semantic Web]] ideals expressed by [[Tim Berners-Lee]].<ref>[http://pubs.acs.org/4librarians/livewire/2008/9.3/news1.html ACS Publications News]</ref><ref>{{YouTube|id=bvgM6TEArOQ|title=Professor Henry Rzepa discusses the launch of Imperial College London's iTunes U}}, Imperial College London</ref><ref>{{YouTube|title=Chemical Science and Data Repository Design with Prof. Henry Rzepa|id=bOkpf7SeNQ8}}, Science & Engineering South</ref>

He is responsible for unraveling the mechanistic origins of stereocontrol in a variety of [[catalytic]] [[polymerisation]] reactions, including that of [[lactide]] to polylactide, a new generation of bio-sustainable polymer not dependent on oil. He is also known for the integration of chemistry (in the form of CML) with emergent Internet technologies and trends such as [[RSS (file format)|RSS]] and [[podcasting]], for the introduction of the Chemical [[MIME]] types in 1994, and for organizing the ECTOC online conferences in [[organic chemistry]], which ran from 1995 to 1998.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rzepa |first=Henry S. |date=1998-03-13 |title=Electronic Conferences on Trends in Organic Chemistry |url=https://www.ch.ic.ac.uk/ectoc/ |access-date=2024-01-15 |website=www.ch.ic.ac.uk |language=English}}</ref>

===Awards and honours===
Rzepa was awarded the [[Herman Skolnik Award]] in 2012 by the [[American Chemical Society]].<ref name=skol>{{cite web|author=Anon|year=2011|title=CCL Archives|url=http://www.ccl.net/cgi-bin/ccl/message-new?2011+09+26+014|website=ccl.net}}</ref>
